title: Alexander Pours Out the Water in the Desert
text:
In 325 BC Alexander the Great led part of his army back from India through the Gedrosian desert, in what is now southern Iran and Pakistan. The march was a disaster. Men and animals died of heat and thirst, and the army moved at night to escape the sun.

Arrian, writing in the second century AD from earlier sources, tells a story he places on this march. The army was suffering badly from thirst, and Alexander, on foot like his men, was leading the column. Some light-armed soldiers who had gone searching found a little water in a shallow gully. They collected it with difficulty, poured it into a helmet, and brought it to the king.

Alexander thanked them, took the helmet, and in full view of the army poured the water out on the ground. Arrian says the whole army was so heartened by this that it was as if every man had drunk what Alexander poured away.

Arrian notes that some writers placed the incident elsewhere, but he praised the act itself as proof of Alexander's endurance and his skill as a general.
lesson: When you lead people through hardship, refusing a comfort they cannot share is often worth more than the comfort itself.
source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, Book 6, chapter 26
caveat: Arrian himself notes that other writers placed this story elsewhere in Alexander's campaigns.
